I train managers in many international companies, and the question I hear most is this: how do I give feedback without hurting people? Many managers use the feedback sandwich. First you give some praise, then you give the constructive criticism, and then you finish with something positive again. It works, but only if you do it well. The biggest mistake is to make the middle of the sandwich too small. If the problem is hidden between two compliments, the other person does not hear it. So be specific. Do not say, your report was not good. Say, the numbers on page two were from last month. Talk about the work, not about the person. That way, people do not take it personally, and they do not get defensive. And remember that being tactful is not the same as being vague. You can be kind and clear at the same time. Blunt feedback hurts, and vague feedback does not help anybody.

When I started my career in Santos, I worked for a trader called Mrs. Lima. After my first big presentation, she called me to her office. I was nervous. She said that my slides were very clear, and that the client had liked my numbers. Then she told me that I spoke too fast, and that I never looked at the audience. I felt terrible, and I tried to explain. She smiled and said that I was getting defensive. She told me that the feedback was about the presentation, not about me. Then she said that she would watch my next presentation and give me one more tip. That was fifteen years ago. Today I have a team of six people, and when I give feedback, I always remember her words. Praise first, be clear about the problem, and always offer help.

Do you have a minute? I'd like to give you some feedback on the report. First, you did a great job with the numbers. They were very clear. I want to point out one thing: the report was two days late. Next time, please tell me early if you need more time. Don't take it personally. It's a small thing. Overall, it was a great first report. Keep up the good work!
